what_it_does: When current flows through a chip's wiring, the resistance of those tiny metal wires causes a small but real voltage drop (called IR drop, from Ohm's law: voltage = current times resistance). If the drop is too large in some spots, transistors in that region receive less power than expected and may behave incorrectly. Predicting where these problematic drops will occur before manufacturing is important but computationally slow. This paper trains a neural network to predict IR drop from the chip's layout image. The novelty is combining two types of neural networks: a convolutional network (CNN, good at reading spatial patterns from images) and a graph neural network (GNN, good at following how cells are connected to each other in a network). The CNN captures broad spatial patterns of power consumption; the GNN follows the actual wire topology of the power delivery network. Combining both gives more accurate predictions, and transfer learning (starting from a model trained on one chip type and fine-tuning with just a few examples from a new chip) makes it practical for real circuits.
